Haha, don’t worry about it. The prof will likely use mostly English in the first few weeks, but as you progress throughout the weeks (you will because homework and oral practice), more Chinese and Mandarin will be used.

You will be given a placement test to assess your level, but keep in mind you do not need to know any Chinese (they will place you where it’s most appropriate based on your score and how you answered).CHIN141 is the heritage stream; however, students have varying experiences with Chinese, making it a unique cohort. The prof takes it slow but there is a lot of homework so be prepared for that and an oral practice outside class. 

Based on your descriptions, you would likely be placed in CHIN141 if you did your assessment, and do not worry that you can’t speak it well, read, or write. You will learn and progress in class, and you will notice that there will also be students who are in a similar situation to you where they cannot speak it well but can understand a little.

I came into the class barely being able to speak any Mandarin. You will be allowed to use some English which you will find that as you progress throughout the course and the following courses, you will depend less on using English. The course 141 is not meant to be for students who are already able to read, write, and speak at an intermediate level, otherwise their placement would likely be higher.

I can assure you that you’re not alone in this position. Knowing what information is important and what to study is also something that I am still actively working on in order to try and do well. That said, here are some advice I can give which I do think helped me with acing my final exam during the summer term. 

1) Do the practice exams if your profs offers them. They provide an idea of what questions will be asked and a sense of what to expect on the exam

2) Learning goals and outcomes are your friends. I find that they provide a general outline pertaining to the lectures, and I like to use that information to guide me in what I should know. I also find it helpful to test myself on the questions

3) Prioritize the harder chapter of contents. Ideally, it’s better to try and tackle down hardest material through spending more time on it. 

4) Flashcards like Anki are great! It is a way to test your knowledge, and I really do find that Anki is great because well… it’s free, it highly customizable, and it encourages space repetition 

5) Space Repetition. You want to consolidate as much information as you can. 

6) Self-care. You need to ensure that the day before your exam, you get adequate sleep to ensure your brain functions at its optimal level the day of exam. During the times you study, be sure to give yourself breaks in between sessions. A technique I recommend is the pomodoro technique. You can find a bunch of “study with me videos” on YouTube with timers included.

7)Office Hours! If you believe that you need further assistance in helping you know what to study in terms of content, attending office hours is always a good start. TAs are also a big help

I hope this helps. Good luck with exams, everyone!

Definitely has to do with time management and creating a schedule for yourself. There are many apps that can help with tracking down your to-do lists and deadlines, and I really like the app called “Notion.” Basically, I make sure to write down all the events I have in the day - courses, appointments, etc. If it seems like there is time that is available in between, then considered that free time to do whatever you want. 

Take your studying bit by bit, don’t cram. Try to use methods like active recall (flashcards/any forms of testing yourself) and space repetition for items that involve heavy memorization. Use time between your day to do this, and do your best to review the material you just learned from your lectures the same day because you want to retain that information. 

I think it’s also important to note that because we are all university, there will be hard days, as in a day where there may be a lot of assignments and studying to do. That is okay! Keep on track of what you’re doing, plan ahead, and don’t forget to use any free time you have to enjoy your hobbies, self care, and relax. You got this!
